42.1 i ntroduction
This chapter is a proposal on how to build and evaluate models for solving problems, espe-
cially when applying the multiple regression approach. Basically the proposed steps are:
First specify the problem, complete with identifying and screening of the variables. The
chosen variables must be correlated to the problem under study and readily accessible. By
carefully studying a correlation matrix for all independent and dependent variables for cur-
rently maintained data, the researcher is allowed to run pilot tests on simple regression
models. These preliminary tests enable insight into future modeling efforts. This is also a
good time to establish goals for the project complete with estimates for project completion
requirements such as necessary time and cost.
Next a model, or several models to be followed, needs to be developed by selecting a best
representative model, using correlation analysis, the researcher should study the interrela-
tionships between various independent variables. Out of this effort, the researcher will be
able to select independent variables in regression equations, as well as transformed inde-
pendent variables that may be used in the final results. Study of residual plots should also be
performed at this time. Finally, once a useful model has been chosen, then procedures for
verification of the model and model maintenance should be started.
This chapter and the header article are an attempt to illustrate the model-building process.
Special emphasis is on procedures for selecting variables for a regression analysis as well as
choosing a best regression model for a specific study. The process follows a personal data
analysis methodology recommended by Katrina D. Maxwell in Applied Statistics for Soft-
ware Managers published by Pearson Publications, Inc. (2002). Maxwell’s text provides not
only a personal data analysis methodology, or a model building process, but illustrates the
process using actual corporate data to solve specific software productivity, time-to-market,
and maintenance problems.
42.2 s ample s tudy
Study Forecasting Gold Prices Using Multiple Linear Regression Method by Ismail, Yahya,
and Shabri, found at http://www.scipub.org/fulltext/ajas/ajas681509-1514.pdf. Both this arti-
cle and the material found in this chapter illustrate and outline the steps for constructing
linear models. Linear models tend to crystallize one’s thinking with regard to the variables
operating in an experimental situation. Models form the basis for the analysis and interpreta-
tion of data generated by the experiments. Therefore, the model should undergo a prelimi-
nary analysis as well as be validated.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 42.3 Lessons Learned
chunks.content:
42.3 Lessons Learned
It usually takes a number of years to collect enough software project data to analyze. Add
the software industry’s high job turnover rate, and more often than not, you will be analyzing
data that was collected by others. What methods should you use? What should you do first?
42.3.1 s tep 1: v alidate your data
Data validation is reviewing the data to determine that it is the right data for the
study and that the values are correctly specified and fit the variable’s scope.
Data validation is the most important step, as it is critical to verify that the specific data is
complete, accurate, and fit. Data is often assembled from various sources, and it needs to be
evaluated to make sure it was gathered correctly and that it adequately represents that for
which it was gathered.
A Judgment Analysis (JAN) study is used throughout this chapter for discussing model con-
struction. Consider the following study, which was generated by a research request from the
College of Business Administration at Omega University. The Information Systems Depart-
ment wanted to find and measure a set of criteria that would be descriptive of the doc-
toral candidate selection process by the IS faculty. This set of criteria would be descriptive
of the candidates’ success in the program. Selective procedures for doctoral candidates in
IS involve looking at many predictor variables; some of these variables are GRE popula-
tion, GMAT scores, Miller Analogies Test (MAT) scores, Strong Vocational Interest Blank
(SVIB), incoming GPA, and previous major field of study. The MMPI is also required for
each incoming doctoral candidate. However, in the past many of the doctoral graduates did
not take the MMPI. Because of this, the 13 subscales of the MMPI were not included in
the study. To describe the doctoral candidate selection process used by the IS faculty, three
questions had to be answered:
n How many distinct judgmental policies are presented among the IS faculty with
respect to what they consider the important cognitive and affective skills of an
outstanding graduate student?
n Which of the affective and cognitive skills being considered for each graduate do the
faculty deem most important?
n Which predictor variables used in determining admission to the program relate to the
captured judgmental policy or policies?

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 42.3.1.1 Statement of Problem
chunks.content:
42.3.1.1 Statement of Problem
At present there seems to be a wide variety of methodologies available to capture and ana-
lyze judgmental policies where either the investigator is looking only at predictor variables
alone or there is one criterion variable and several predictor variables. The author has been
unable to find in the literature a methodology for capturing and analyzing judgmental poli-
cies where the investigator is looking at a set of criterion variables and a set of predictor
variables in conjunction. Therefore, the problem was to attempt to capture and analyze
540 n n n r e S earch Metho DS for I N for M at I o N Sy S te MS n ch apter 42
judgmental policies of the IS faculty while looking at both a set of criterion variables and a
set of predictor variables.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 42.3.1.2 Purpose
chunks.content:
42.3.1.2 Purpose
The basic purpose of this study, which was service-oriented in nature, was to develop a
methodology for capturing and analyzing judgmental policies where the investigator is look-
ing at a set of criterion variables and a set of predictors in conjunction. This type of meth-
odology was needed so that the technique can be used to a great degree in judgmental
research.
42.3.2 s tep 2: s elect the variables and model
Variable and model selection determines what variables and relationships to study
to ensure all steps taken target the intended purpose of the study.
The purpose for variable and model selection is to determine what data we actually have and
the semantics of the data. What relationships could we study? What possible relationships
should we study? What relationships will we study first? Your answers will depend on the
overall goals of the analysis.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 42.3.2.1 Operational Definitions
chunks.content:
42.3.2.1 Operational Definitions
In this section, we provide definitions of various concepts discussed throughout this
chapter.
Ipsative JAN refers to the JAN approach in which the judges were using personal knowledge
of the capabilities of each IS doctoral graduate to suggest a rank. It is a way of quantifying
subjective opinions that yields more objective results.
The judges are only those faculty who have had the student as an advisee or student, or
worked on special projects with him and rated the student using the criterion instrument.
The judgmental evaluation procedure is the outcome of a rating process by a judge who has
been presented a series of variables on which he must base a decision. For example, how
does a judge involve effective thought processing when presented with a series of variables
on which he must base a decision?
Normative JAN refers to the JAN approach in which the judges were utilizing the predictor
variables to rank each IS student into one of seven categories.
A profile score is a profile that was defined as the set of ratings assigned by a judge to a spe-
cific IS doctoral student on the nine criteria, Y
i
, i = l, ... , 9.
Type A JAN is an analysis in which all the judges give judgments on the same subjects with
respect to the same criterion variable and predictor variables.
Type B JAN is an analysis in which the judges do not judge the same subjects (different
judges could judge a different number of subjects also) with respect to the same criterion
variable and predictor variables.

chunks.heading: 42.3.2.2 Questions Answered
chunks.content:
42.3.2.2 Questions Answered
The questions answered were subdivided into two general populations. The first population
of concern pertains to how well the methodology answered the questions of the IS research
request. These questions are as follows:
n How many different judgmental policies exist within the IS Department concerning
what constitutes an outstanding IS doctoral graduate?
n Which of the affective and cognitive skills being considered for each graduate do the
faculty deem most important?
n What kinds of information that they now collect are important indicators of a
graduate’s ability to succeed as an IS employee?
The second population of concern involves interpretation of computer outputs. The major
questions that were considered are as follows:
n What type of judgmental policies are captured?
n Is it possible to determine whether or not each judge is a “good” judge?
n How many judgmental policies are captured?
n What are the most important predictor and criterion variables?
n What is the relationship between the criteria and predictors of importance?
n Is the procedure for analyzing a captured policy an intuitive or a statistical process?

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 42.3.2.4 Judgment Analysis
chunks.content:
42.3.2.4 Judgment Analysis
The Judgment Analysis technique is useful for identifying the rating policies existing in a
board or committee of judges. With this technique, each judge makes a judgmental decision
on one common criterion variable on which he is given a common predictor set profile on a
set of judges to determine how many different evaluation policies exist in the group. Next,
a multiple regression analysis can be made to determine the composition of each captured
policy.
The JAN procedure consists of two basic stages. In the first stage, a least-squares solution
of a multiple regression equation is computed for each judge, which predicts the criterion
decision he has made. It answers the question of how consistent the judge is in his use of
specific variables in arriving at an overall decision by giving his decision-making equation
and the R
2
, the square of the multiple correlation coefficient, from his multiple regression
analysis. A high R
2
indicates that he has a policy and was consistent in expressing it through
his criterion decisions.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: chapter 42 n a Metho D o L o G y for Mo D e L c o NS truct I o N n n n 543
chunks.content:
chapter 42 n a Metho D o L o G y for Mo D e L c o NS truct I o N n n n 543
Next, a hierarchical grouping procedure is initiated that allows the grouping of individual
judges according to some objective function by similarity of their decision-making equations
in this case. Groupings are selected that yield the smallest decrease in ability to predict the
criterion from knowledge of which individual judges are in a particular group (loss in R
2
).
The first step in the grouping procedure reduces the number of equations by one. The two
judges whose decision-making equations are most similar are grouped together as a unit and
all other judges are left ungrouped. From the set of ungrouped judges, the process then
selects a judge whose decision-making equation is most similar to that of the grouped judges
and groups him with them as a unit. The number of judges remaining in the ungrouped set
is reduced by one at each step of the process until all judges have been grouped into a single
unit. At each step of the grouping process, an examination of the loss of predictive efficiency
allows the investigator to identify the number of various judgmental policies that exist.
If a single policy is characteristic of the whole collection of judges, it can be determined at
the final stage of grouping. If a joint policy does not exist, arbitration of the criterion by the
whole group may yield a joint policy.
Judgment analysis has been extensively used by the United States Air Force to analyze indi-
vidual and group judgments and to formulate common or overall judgmental policies. A large
amount of this type of work has been done by Ward, Bottenberg, and Christal. Bottenberg
and Christal
1
were originally responsible for the mathematical and computer program devel-
opments in the field.
2
S howed that JAN was highly valid.
42.3.3 s tep 3: p erform preliminary analyses
Preliminary analysis is a review of the data to become more familiar with its parts,
descriptions, and relationships, in order to make sure it will not violate any of the
assumptions the statistical tests are built on.
The purpose of the preliminary analysis is to check that the assumptions underlying the sta-
tistical tests are true. You need to objectively look at the data and decide on the goal for the
study. You must determine which of the variables collected has an influence on achieving this
goal. The preliminary analysis will utilize different types of graphs, tables, correlations, and
other statistical tools.

Each of the criteria was scored on a scale from 1 to 5 where 1 = poor, 2 = below average,
3 = average, 4 = above average, and 5 = outstanding.
The criterion instrument included in the faculty questionnaire was developed by three mem-
bers of the IS faculty. Considerations for the instrument were based on the following ques-
tion. “If it were my job to hire a Ph.D. with a degree in IS work, what characteristics or
attributes would I would expect him to have?” From this question, the nine criterion vari-
ables were generated and used in the study. Most of the IS doctorates have graduated in the
past three years and so consideration was not given to the number of publications, employ-
ment effectiveness in their present job, and professional affiliations.
The criterion instrument was submitted to the 16 members of the IS faculty with the follow-
ing instructions: Please rate each of the above Ph.D. graduates with whom you are familiar
on a scale from 1 to 5 where 1 = poor, 2 = below average, 3 = average, 4 = above average, and
5 = outstanding. The basis for comparison should be your conception of what constitutes an
outstanding Ph.D. graduate in IS.
Notice that this is an ipsative type of JAN ranking. Approximately 500 ratings were obtained
through the distribution of the questionnaire.

40 sets of ratings were randomly selected. The modified Q-sort instrument with the neces-
sary instructions was then distributed to the 13 faculty members of the IS faculty and to the 3
past members of the IS faculty. Instruments were returned by 12 of the 16 faculty members.

By design and methodologies for a study, the designer identifies and enables the
control, as well as the interpretation of the sources of variation in the study.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 42.3.4.1 Subjects Judged
chunks.content:
42.3.4.1 Subjects Judged
The IS Department had its first doctoral graduate 10 years earlier. Since then, not including
the previous year’s graduates, 55 individuals have received their doctoral degree from the
IS Department. Of these 55 graduates, it was possible to get complete information on the
predictor variables for 50 of them. These 50 were the individuals used in the study.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 42.3.4.2 Judges
chunks.content:
42.3.4.2 Judges
At present, there are 13 faculty members of the IS Department who have worked with some
or all of the 50 doctoral graduates. There were three faculty members on the staff of the IS
Department over the 10 years who have left for positions in other universities. Since they are
familiar with many of the graduates being studied, they were included in the study. These 16
past or present faculty members were used as judges.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 42.3.4.3 Strategy Used for Obtaining Data
chunks.content:
42.3.4.3 Strategy Used for Obtaining Data
Procedure 1
Out of the approximately 500 sets of ratings obtained on the criterion instrument, 40 were
randomly selected.
Procedure 2
Each of the 16 members of the IS faculty were asked to do a modified Q-sort on the 40 sets of
ratings. Each set of ratings was called a profile. They were asked to compare the 40 profiles
against one another and place them in seven groups. Group 7 would represent those pro-
files they considered the best of the group of 40 and group 1 would represent those profiles
they considered the poorest in the group of 40. Groups 2 through 6 lay on an ordinal scale
550 n n n r e S earch Metho DS for I N for M at I o N Sy S te MS n ch apter 42
between one and seven. The only restrictions were that each judge must place at least one
profile in each of the seven groups. Hopefully, this forced the 12 judges to think along the
whole continuum. The instrument and the instructions used for the Q-sort were presented
to the IS faculty in a training session before they actually conducted this part of the study.
Procedure 3
After the judges completed the rankings, a Type A JAN was run to determine the number
of judgmental policies. The decision as to the number of policies existing was based on the
following consideration: Any judge who was unable to identify at least one significant factor
is failing to relate any predictor variable set to any criterion variable.
Procedure 4
